caption:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued OpenAI and Sam Altman, saying ChatGPT was sold as safe while its risks were kept quiet.
The state wants minors blocked from ChatGPT and outside approval for every new model in Texas.
OpenAI says it worked with experts to build safeguards.

Should a state get to approve new AI models before they launch?

paragraphs.text: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued OpenAI and its chief executive, Sam Altman, on Friday, October 23, 2026, accusing the company of deceiving Texans about the safety of ChatGPT. The suit was filed in Collin County district court, according to The Texas Tribune and Courthouse News Service.

The 67-page complaint names OpenAI Global, LLC, affiliated OpenAI entities and Altman personally as defendants. It relies on two state laws: the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices-Consumer Protection Act and the Securing Children Online through Parental Empowerment Act, known as the SCOPE Act, which sets age verification and parental consent requirements for digital platforms.
What the state is asking for

Texas is seeking a broad injunction. According to The Texas Tribune, it would require OpenAI to block minors from using ChatGPT and would require a court-appointed evaluator to approve new models, along with other restrictions. Courthouse News Service reported that the state wants to bar OpenAI from releasing new ChatGPT models in Texas without approval from an independent evaluator named by the court.

The complaint also asks for monetary relief of more than $1 million, according to America News Nation. The Texan reported that the suit seeks to hold Altman personally liable, both for the alleged violations and for statements he has made about the company's products.

The state argues that OpenAI marketed ChatGPT as safe, accurate and reliable while failing to warn users about its risks. Paxton's office said in a press release that mass shooters had been aided, that vulnerable people had been encouraged toward suicide and that minors had become addicted to the chatbot. The office attributed those harms to what it called the company's drive to win the AI race.

According to Courthouse News Service, the complaint cites at least eight cases of people who committed violent acts after consulting ChatGPT, including the 2025 Florida State University shooting, an example drawn from a separate lawsuit filed by a victim's widow. Jonathan Stone, chief of the attorney general's Consumer Protection Division, wrote that the design of the chatbot encourages use by adolescents.

The suit further claims that ChatGPT lacks adequate age verification and parental oversight, that children can share sensitive personal data without enough protection, and that OpenAI cannot fully control its technology. It points to AI agent incidents and a July 2026 security breach at Hugging Face, according to America News Nation and Courthouse News Service.

In a statement, Paxton said OpenAI has a responsibility to protect users and warn them about the dangers of its platform, and that he would work to make sure powerful technology companies are not above the law.
OpenAI's response and the political backdrop

An OpenAI spokesperson told The Texas Tribune that the company worked with experts to reduce risks and build safeguards. The statement said governments should help set AI safety standards and that OpenAI wants to work with Texas and other states on rules that apply to the whole industry rather than to a single company.

Paxton is running for the US Senate against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico. Campaign finance filings show Elon Musk, who competes with Altman through his company xAI, spent nearly $200 million on ads supporting Paxton's campaign, according to Courthouse News Service. The state is represented by outside counsel that includes Tony Buzbee, who defended Paxton during his 2023 impeachment proceedings.

Texas is not the first state to take OpenAI to court over safety claims. Florida sued the company in June, and America News Nation reported that several other states have filed similar suits. In the past year, Paxton has also sued or settled with Meta, TikTok, Snapchat and Roblox under consumer protection laws.

The request for a court-appointed evaluator reaches beyond the product people use today. It asks a court to sit between OpenAI and the release of future models in one state. If a judge grants any part of it, Texas would gain a direct say over when new AI systems reach the public there.
The next step to watch is OpenAI's formal answer in Collin County and whether the court considers any early order on minors' access to ChatGPT while the case proceeds.
